Observations to test:
1. A base-0 task gave no completion signal and shaped reward never lifted one (confirmed); count task_completed rollouts (shaped>0 is not a completion) before spending on it.
2. Training one task shifts others; and the submitted adapter serves EVERY task, so it can regress one you never evaluated (incl. eval-only, base 0). Eval a candidate and the FINAL stack on every task before submitting.
3. On equal-reward rollouts, changing the start state or reward beat training longer.
4. Adapter pairs combined well and badly -- evaluate each adapter alone AND the pair in one batch. One session chained (train B from A's adapter) to compound gains where fresh adapters only paired (unconfirmed).
5. Gains flattened after moderate steps -- read the curve before extending. One run kept past its peak (reward falling) lost its gain and hurt other tasks (unconfirmed); cancel keeps the last saved step.
6. Training-seed scores and held-out dev evals have differed; prefer the held-out number.
7. Queues took hours; submit the jobs wanted together then wait in LONG windows (waiting isn't charged), not short re-polls.
8. Keep the best checked stack loaded as you go, so a cut-short session still has one.
9. Plan the budget up front (reserve checking evals/loads); commit early to tasks with signal.
10. The biggest gain came from training the highest-HEADROOM task (low base, real signal), not the strong ones (unconfirmed).
11. A second train on another signal-bearing task added to the first; stopping while a train+checks still fit left it untested (unconfirmed).
12. An eval that ended with no count says nothing about the adapter; a rerun cost less than dropping it (unconfirmed).

Did not work in earlier sessions:
- A practice start state the evaluation never uses (cube already in hand): almost no successful rollouts.
- A training-only note did not carry to evaluation; it edits only the prompt text (trainer doc), not the task trained.

Relative paths in SPEC (a reward file, an init adapter path, data files) resolve against the workspace, where `train.py` runs, wherever SPEC itself is. The programs can call exactly the functions listed under `APIs:` in the task's eval_prompt.txt. The Key rules of the stack, revstack, stackv2 and handover prompts also name `get_object_pose`, `sample_grasp_pose`, `goto_pose_arm*` and a `z_approach` parameter: none of these exists in these cells (the rules text is shared with the tasks' privileged-API variant). The prompts are the benchmark's cells of record and are scored as they are. A stack (`eval.py --adapter A,B`, `load.py stack`) holds at most 4 adapters: each is rank 32 and the serving's maximum LoRA rank is 128; a larger stack ends `failed` with `stack rank 160 > 128 (the serving's --max-lora-rank): at most 4 adapters of rank 32`. Your shell on this site writes only in the workspace and has no network (pip, curl and similar fail) and no Slurm client; all compute goes through train.py and eval.py. ## What a practice call is GRPO on LoRA adapters of the policy model named in SCOREBOARD.md's `policy:` line (LoRA rank 32, alpha 64, on q,k,v,o,out,gate,up,down projections for Qwen3.8-27B; other policies have no `out`). Each step: `batch` prompts x 8 rollouts. GRPO's update comes from reward differences among a prompt's 8 rollouts: a prompt whose rollouts all get the same reward adds nothing to it. A rollout is one program written by the model for the task, run once in the task's simulator on one seed; its score is the reward below. The training prompt is the task's evaluation prompt, byte for byte (checked before training), unless the spec sets `note` or `goal` or a `data` row sets `prompt`: those are part of the training prompt only. Every eval, including the final hidden-seed score, uses the task's `tasks//eval_prompt.txt` in the workspace verbatim, without any note or goal. Sampling during practice: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20; at most 8192 generated tokens per program. Sampling during evaluation (eval.py and the final score): temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, presence_penalty 1.5, thinking off; at most 8192 generated tokens per program (envs/capx/config_of_record_v4.yaml). For lift, stack, wipe and nut the practice unit and the eval cell run the same task config (`*_reduced_api_exampleless.yaml` is the s4:paper cell's config). A policy whose name carries `+init:` (SCOREBOARD.md's `policy:` line) is the model plus that init adapter: its base is served with the init, every train without `init` starts from it, so each trained adapter already contains the init's change, and a stack of two such adapters applies that change twice. ## Spec fields (a spec with any other field fails; see Failures) | field | type | default | accepted | |---|---|---|---| | `task` | string or list | required unless `data` | a trainable task (see workspace/tasks/INDEX.md), or a list of them: one call practising all, every batch split equally across them (`batch` a multiple of their number; no `note` / `goal`); revstack practises alone | | `name` | string | `a` | letters, digits, `_ . -`, at most 48; not already taken, not `base` / `loaded`. Single-adapter mode: omit it (or `current`) | | `steps` | integer | 1 | any positive integer (cost grows with it, see below) | | `batch` | integer | 8 | prompts per step (each x 8 rollouts) | | `lr` | float | 2e-5 | learning rate | | `init` | string | none (fresh LoRA) | an adapter name produced by an earlier train of this session (`base` is not one: omit `init` to start from the policy). Single-adapter mode: omit it (or `current`); every train continues `current`. The new adapter is the init adapter continued (it already holds init's change): loading both stacks that change twice | | `start_preset` | string | none | a named start-state preset (core/start_presets.py: `restack_grasped`/`restack_lifted`/`restack_aligned`, `nut_grasped`/`nut_aligned`) to begin practice from an intermediate scene (e.g. object already grasped) so the agent trains the hard tail; the staged reward then scores only the stages after that sub-goal; fails loudly if the preset has not been built. With hidden tasks (B2): also the name of a preset you built with `preset.py` (`presets/.json`), on the task it was built on; on a hidden task only such a preset | | `start_mix` | string | none | a mixed start-state pool (core/mix_presets.py, built with `build_mix`): seeds split across presets of one task at a ratio, some from scratch; the staged reward scores the full chain; not with `start_preset`; fails loudly if not built; refused on a hidden task (B2) | | `reward` | string | `task_completed` | `task_completed` (1.0 if the task's own success check passes, else 0.0); `shaped` (the simulator's staged reward); Python source containing `def reward(r)`; or the path of a `.py` file (relative paths: the workspace) defining `reward(r)`. `r` is the simulator's reply: `task_completed`, `reward`, `sandbox_rc`, `seed`, `log_tail` (keys or attributes); return a float | | `seed_start` | integer | 810001 | rollout k of the call runs on seed `seed_start + k`; must not reach seeds 1-100 | | `note` | string | none | one sentence inserted after the training prompt's Goal line (not a comment: the rollouts see it; evaluation prompts never have it) | | `goal` | string | none | replaces the training prompt's Goal line (evaluation prompts keep theirs) | | `time` | string | set by the site: 1 GPU 25 min + 13 min x steps, 2 GPUs 85 min + 17 min x steps, 3 GPUs 30 min + 14 min x steps, at least 2 h (whole minutes, rounded up; the job record's `config` shows the value used) | wall limit of each Slurm job of the call, `HH:MM:SS`; a call whose job reaches it continues from its last saved step (below); once it has continued 3 times it keeps the adapter of its last saved step, as a cancel (result `time_limit`; a preempted or node-failed call likewise, result `preempted` / `node_fail`), or ends `failed` with the fact if none was saved | | `data` | string | none | a JSONL file of training prompts in your workspace: see Training data below. With `data`, the tasks, seeds, order and steps come from its rows | | `objective` | string | `grpo` | `grpo` (the practice call above) or `sft` (supervised fine-tuning on your own demonstrations: see SFT below; its spec has `data` and the fields of that section only) | | `epochs` | integer | 1 | `objective: sft` only: passes over the kept rows | | `min_reward` | number | 1.0 | `objective: sft` only: rows with `reward` >= this are trained on, the others dropped (a filter, never a weight) | ## Training data (`data`) `data` names a JSONL file in your workspace (a path relative to the workspace, or absolute inside it): one line per training prompt, `{"task": ..., "seed": ..., "variant": ..., "prompt": ...}` (`variant` and `prompt` optional, no other keys): - `task`: a trainable task. `variant`: another trainable task of the same simulator task (e.g. `stack` with variant `revstack`; revstack runs under a scene shift and practises alone, so a dataset with revstack rows has no rows of any other task); the row then trains on `variant`. Any mixture of tasks and variants is allowed. - `seed`: an integer >= 810001 (seeds 1-100 are the final score's, 800001-809999 are eval.py's dev seeds); all 8 rollouts of the row run on that seed. - `prompt`: replaces the task's user message for that row only (the system message stays). A row without `prompt` trains on the task's eval prompt, checked byte for byte before training; a row with `prompt` is not checked and counts as a prompt override, a method choice recorded with the adapter (`data.prompt_overrides` and `data.label` in training.json). - Rows train in file order, `batch` rows per step: the row count must be a multiple of `batch`, and the call runs rows / batch steps (omit `steps`, or give that number). The call's tasks come from the rows (omit `task`); `note` and `goal` are not accepted with `data`. At most 4096 rows, 16 MB, 65536 characters per `prompt`. - The file is copied when the call starts; training.json's `resolved_spec.data` and the train's result (`config.data`) record its `sha256`, `rows`, rows per task (`tasks`) and `prompt_overrides`. ## SFT (`objective: sft`) A spec `{"objective": "sft", "data": ".jsonl"}` (optional: `name`, `init`, `epochs` (1), `batch` (16 rows per step), `lr` (1e-4), `min_reward` (1.0), `time`; no other field) trains the policy's LoRA by supervised fine-tuning (cross-entropy on the program's tokens only; LoRA rank 32 / alpha 64 on the policy's modules, or `init` continued; without `init` it continues the policy's own init, as a practice call does). It runs on the small policy profiles (SCOREBOARD.md's `policy:` line names one, e.g. Qwen3-8B). - Each line of `data` is `{"task": ..., "seed": ..., "prompt": [{"role": "system" | "user", "content": ...}, ...], "program": ..., "reward": ...}` (exactly these keys): `task` a trainable task (a hidden task by the name you see), `prompt` the chat the program answers (the user message last; `tasks//eval_prompt.txt` as messages is the eval prompt of record), `program` the response trained on, `reward` a number used only as the `min_reward` filter. - `seed` is the scene the program ran on: seeds 1-100 (the final score's) and 800001-809999 (eval.py's dev seeds) are refused, so no reading you or the final score take is on a scene the policy was fitted on. - A kept row whose prompt is not the task's eval prompt of record is a prompt override (a method choice): counted in `data.prompt_overrides` and labelled, as `note`/`goal` are. - Steps = ceil(kept rows x epochs / batch); rows train in a fixed shuffled order; a row longer than 4096 tokens is dropped (`call.json` `sft_facts.dropped_too_long`). At most 20000 rows, 256 MB, 65536 characters per message or program. - Building the file: `python3 skills/trainer/sft_rows.py practice adapters/ [--min-reward 1] [--steps 3-5] > sft.jsonl` takes a finished practice call's rollouts (Output below); `python3 skills/trainer/sft_rows.py rollouts rollouts/.jsonl [--min-reward 1] > sft.jsonl` takes rollout.py rows (reward = your self_reward). Both print why each dropped row was dropped. - Output: `adapters//` with the adapter, `sft_log.json` (per step: `step`, `loss`, `grad_norm`, `tokens`), `call.json` and `training.json` (`resolved_spec.data`: `sha256` of your file, `rows`, `kept`, rows per task, `min_reward`, `prompt_overrides`); the train's result shows the same under `config.data`. A cancel or a cluster stop keeps nothing (the adapter is saved at the end). - Cost: 1 GPU x (0.05 + 0.000695 x steps x batch) canonical GPU-hours (the admission estimate counts every row of the file). ## Failures A request this site cannot run as written ends `failed` in `jobs/.json` with this text; An all-zero update is a training outcome, shown on the scoreboard: the adapter's change is zero, so it behaves as its init (base or the init adapter). ## Progress and cancel While a train runs, its record shows completed steps, the latest step's mean reward, the fraction of rollouts with reward > 0 and canonical GPU-hours of the steps done so far (read from the trainer's per-step output about once a minute). A checkpoint is saved every step. A call stopped by the cluster (time limit, preemption, node failure) continues from its last checkpoint in a new Slurm job, at most 3 times; its status then says `continued from step k in job J`, and its result lists every Slurm job (`jobs`) and each continuation (`continued`: `job` stopped, `cause`, `from` step, `of` steps, `continued_in` job), as it lists site retries. `cancel.py ID` stops the job and keeps the adapter of the last saved step (registered with the steps it ran), or ends the job `failed` if none was saved; either way the job is charged the canonical cost of the steps it completed (see Cost). ## Cost (canonical GPU-hours) The budget is charged a canonical cost per call, the same whatever hardware the site runs the call on. The tables below are the Qwen3.8-27B policy's; with another policy the costs differ, and SCOREBOARD.md's "Expected cost per call" line gives them. | call | canonical cost | |---|---| | train, 1 step | 2.76 | | train, 10 steps | 4.03 | | train, 30 steps | 6.84 | | train, N steps | 2 x (1.31 + 0.0703 x N x batch / 8) | | eval of one task on | 5 seeds | 20 seeds | 100 seeds | |---|---|---|---| | canonical cost | 0.36 | 0.38 | 0.48 | An eval's cost is mostly its fixed part, so 100 seeds cost little more than 5. A call that fails or is cancelled is charged the canonical cost of the steps it completed, or less if it ran only briefly. The cost is also the admission estimate. ## Output A finished train writes `adapters//` (read-only to you): `adapter_model.safetensors`, `adapter_config.json`, `rewards.json` (per step: `step`, `score_mean` over that step's rollouts), `call.json` (job ids, `gpu_hours` = the canonical charge to your budget, `gpu_hours_actual` = measured hardware time, not charged, nonzero LoRA-B count, rollout seed range) and `training.json` (`resolved_spec`: the controls actually used). The adapter can then be named in `eval.py --adapter`, `load.py`, or as `init` of another train. Each `rewards.json` step also has `zero_variance_frac` (the share of that step's prompt groups whose rollouts all got one reward) and `failure_stages` (failed rollouts by stage: `sim`, `timeout`, `program`, `grader`, `task`); the running job's status line shows them for the latest step and the train's result lists them per step (`step_facts`). A call of several tasks (a `task` list, or `data` naming several) adds `per_task` to each `rewards.json` step: `{task: {"score_mean", "rollouts"}}`, that step's rollouts of each task and their mean reward (a rollout is attributed by its prompt; one matching no single task is left out).
